summary: Adds an optional Longest-Match Label Mapping procedure to the Label Distribution Protocol so label switched paths can span multiple IGP areas within one autonomous system. A label may be used when the forwarding equivalence class matches an entry in the routing table, rather than needing an exact match, which lets routes summarized between areas still work for label switching.

plainLanguage.summary: Normally you need the exact street address to deliver a package. This lets routers accept a close-enough match, such as just the town, so deliveries can cross borders between neighborhoods of a big network.

subtitle: An optional LDP rule that lets a router use a label when the route is only a longest-prefix match, so MPLS paths can cross IGP areas without leaking addresses.

tldr.problem: LDP recommends that a label only be used when the routing table has an exact match for the FEC, so MPLS paths across IGP areas needed every router loopback address to be leaked between areas, defeating the point of having areas.
tldr.mechanism: A new optional Longest-Match Label Mapping procedure lets a router use a label if the FEC matches a routing table entry by IP longest match, meaning an exact match or a subset of an entry, provided the advertising router is a next hop.
tldr.outcome: Border routers can aggregate prefixes in the IGP while LDP still builds one contiguous LSP per egress router, with backward compatibility and incremental deployment.

facts.label: Applies to
facts.value: IPv4 and IPv6 prefix FEC elements

facts.label: Match rule
facts.value: Exact match or subset of a RIB entry

today: RFC 5283 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It extends the LDP specification in RFC 5036 as an optional procedure.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Link state IGPs such as OSPF and IS-IS let an autonomous system be split into areas (or levels) to make routing scale. The LDP specification (RFC 5036), however, says that a router receiving a Label Mapping message for a prefix SHOULD NOT use the label for forwarding unless its routing table has an entry that exactly matches the FEC Element.

As a result, MPLS LSPs between Label Edge Routers in different areas are not set up unless the specific loopback addresses (for IPv4, /32 routes) of all those routers are redistributed across all areas. RFC 5283 extends the Label Mapping procedure so contiguous inter-area LSPs can be set up while the area border routers keep aggregating IP prefixes.
sections.plainLanguage: The old rule says a router may only deliver if it has the exact house number. That forces everybody to share every house number with every town, which makes the lists huge.

sections.title: The Problem with Existing Options
sections.content:
Provider MPLS networks keep growing as they add Layer 3 and Layer 2 VPN services, so many providers must introduce IGP areas and still need LSPs between provider edge routers in different areas. The RFC lists three existing ways to do this and the drawbacks of each.

  • LDP with IGP route leaking: every PE loopback is redistributed across area boundaries. The IGP database, RIB and FIB of every router grow, so the benefit of areas is largely lost.
  • BGP over LDP with MPLS hierarchy: needs BGP on all ABRs, cannot locally protect against ABR failures with IP/LDP Fast Reroute, and needs migration effort.
  • Inter-area RSVP-TE: sensible when RSVP-TE is already used, but not desired when LDP is used inside areas and traffic engineering is not needed.

The need, then, is an LDP-based solution that sets up contiguous inter-area LSPs without leaking specific PE loopbacks across area boundaries.
sections.plainLanguage: The old fixes are like making every town keep a copy of every address book, hiring a separate postal service, or building a different kind of road. All of them are heavy for what is needed.

sections.title: The Longest-Match Label Mapping Procedure
sections.content:
The new procedure applies to IPv4 and IPv6 prefix FEC elements. It SHOULD be possible to turn it on and off by configuration, and it SHOULD be off by default. It MAY be possible to enable it per prefix.

When a router receives a Label Mapping message for a prefix FEC element, it SHOULD use the label for MPLS forwarding if its routing table has an entry that matches the FEC and the advertising router is a next hop to reach it. It SHOULD then advertise the same FEC and a label to its LDP peers. A match is an IP longest match: the FEC either equals a RIB entry or is a subset of one. A FEC that is a superset of a RIB entry is not a match.

LDP re-advertises the specific FEC, not the aggregate found in the RIB. Each LSP still follows the IGP shortest path, and FECs are distributed in an ordered way, so an egress failure propagates through Label Withdraw messages.

Because one RIB change can affect many FECs, the router MUST re-check all FECs that are subsets of the changed prefix. When a more specific prefix appears it MUST see whether it is a better match. When a prefix disappears it MUST use another best match if there is one, and otherwise remove the binding and send a Label Withdraw. When a next hop changes it MUST update the forwarding entry of every FEC using that prefix.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of asking for the exact house number, the router accepts the town name if the house is inside it. It still tells the next router the exact house, not just the town.

sections.title: Application Examples
sections.content:
The main example has a backbone area B and two edge areas A and C. In area C the PE routers have loopbacks 192.0.2.1/32, 192.0.2.2/32 and 192.0.2.3/32. ABR1 advertises the aggregate 192.0.2.0/26 into the backbone IGP while still advertising all the specific /32 FEC elements in LDP. ABR2 advertises 192.0.2.0/24 into area A, again with all the /32 FECs in LDP.

The ingress PE4 in area A has only the /24 in its RIB, yet each /32 FEC is a subset of it, so under the new procedure one LSP is established from PE4 to every egress PE in area C while the ABRs keep aggregating.

A second example is a LER dual-connected to two LSRs using static routes. Under RFC 5036 the ingress LER needs one IP route per egress LER and per outgoing interface. With this procedure it only needs one IP route per outgoing interface.
sections.plainLanguage: The far-away town only knows a rough region, but each package still carries the full house number. Because the house is inside the region, the town can send it the right way.

sections.title: Deployment and Convergence
sections.content:
Routers that implement this are backward compatible with RFC 5036 routers. For an end-to-end LSP over aggregated routes, every router in every area that uses aggregation must implement the procedure. If one does not, the LSP started at the egress stops at that router, with no other adverse effects.

It can be deployed incrementally, per area or per routing domain, and routers within an area can be upgraded in any order without disruption. During roll-out, ABRs should keep advertising the specific prefixes until all routers in the area are upgraded, and only then switch to the aggregate alone. The RFC warns that moving from leaking specific loopbacks to aggregation may cause suboptimal routing, as discussed in RFC 2966.

On convergence, the change shrinks the link state database and FIB entries, which helps pure IP routers sharing the IGP, but it does not reduce the number of LFIB entries, so MPLS routers need an additional mechanism such as MPLS hierarchy. For an egress LER failure, applications that track availability may see different behavior, and the RFC suggests relying on LDP ordered label distribution or advertising LER reachability in the IGP without creating FIB entries.
sections.plainLanguage: You can upgrade one neighborhood at a time. Old and new routers can live together, but a path only gets through as far as the last router that understands the new rule.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC states that the Longest-Match Label Mapping procedure does not introduce any change to the Security Considerations section of the LDP specification, RFC 5036. It adds no new security mechanism of its own.

That is the whole of what the text says. Anyone deploying it should therefore apply the security guidance that already applies to LDP.
sections.plainLanguage: This change does not add any new locks or new risks. The same safety rules that LDP already has still apply.

viz.caption: WHAT EACH AREA KNOWS IN THE EXAMPLE (RFC 5283, SECTION 6.1)
WHEN THE RIB CHANGES, THE ROUTER MUST RE-CHECK ITS FECS

items.title: New prefix appears
items.text: Check whether it is a better match for existing FECs; the next hop may change.

items.title: Prefix disappears
items.text: Use another best match if one exists; otherwise remove the binding and send Label Withdraw.

items.title: Next hop changes
items.text: Change the forwarding entry of every FEC using that prefix.
